### Cholesterol-modified siIL11 enhances the efficiency of immunotherapy

Next, to explore the therapeutic effects of targeting IL-11 in modulating tumor immunity, we designed and synthesized a cholesterol-modified siIL11. This stability modification involves attaching cholesterol molecules to the siRNA tail, extending its circulation time, enhancing membrane penetration, and promoting cellular uptake. We then combined it with anti-PD1 or anti-CD8 in tumor-bearing mice, following the schedule in [Figure 7](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#fig7)F. According to the survival analysis results, the mice treated with both anti-PD1 and cholesterol (chol)-siIL11 had a longer survival time than the single-treatment group mice ([Figures 7](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#fig7)G and 7H). The proportion of CD8+ T cells was significantly increased when chol-siIL11 or anti-PD1 was used. Moreover, a higher percentage of CD8+ T cell infiltration in tumors was observed in the combination treatment group than in the single-treatment group ([Figures 7](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#fig7)I and 7J). Almost no CD8+ T cells were detected after anti-CD8 antibody administration. Meanwhile, the proportion of PD1+, TIGIT+, CTLA4+, and TIM3+ CD8+ T cells significantly decreased after chol-siIL11 treatment (combined or not with the anti-PD1 treatment) ([Figures 7](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#fig7)K and [S12](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#mmc1)A). Furthermore, we found an increased T cell proliferative capacity in both the single- and combination-treatment groups, with a more pronounced cell proliferation level restoration in the combination-treatment group ([Figures S12](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#mmc1)B and S12C). Notably, the killing function of CD8+ T cells was restored after the targeted inhibition of IL-11, whose efficacy was like that of the anti-PD1 treatment, and the proportion of IFN-γ+ and granzyme B+ cells increased. The T cell killing function resulting from the combination treatment was significantly higher than that resulting from the single treatment with chol-siIL11 or anti-PD1 ([Figures 7](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#fig7)L and [S12](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#mmc1)D). Conversely, the Ki67 and TUNEL staining results revealed that the treatment with chol-siIL11, combined with anti-PD1 or not, was able to decrease the proliferative capacity and increase the apoptotic capacity of tumor cells ([Figure S12](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#mmc1)E). The above data demonstrate that the treatment with chol-siIL11 to target IL-11 identified here significantly rescued the T cell killing function and improved the efficacy of the anti-PD1 combination treatment.

### H3K9la positively correlates with IL-11 expression and indicates unfavorable immunotherapy response in HNSCC patients

To explore the correlation between IL-11 and H3K9la in clinical settings, we detected the IL-11 and H3K9la expression levels using HNSCC tissue microarray analysis. IL-11 immunoreactivity scores were significantly higher in the H3K9la+ group than the H3K9la−, and IL-11 and H3K9la had markedly positive correlation in HNSCC tissues (_r_= 0.701; [Figure S13](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#mmc1)A). To confirm the role of H3K9la in promoting immunotherapy failure, a multiple immunofluorescence assay revealed that the non-responder patients had higher expression of H3K9la than the responders and more CD8+ T cell infiltration was present in the TME of responders ([Figures 7](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#fig7)M and [S13](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#mmc1)B).

In conclusion, our findings reveal an epigenetic mechanism of lactate-mediated histone lactylation involved in regulating immune escape in a tumor metabolic reprogramming context. We demonstrate the key role of IL-11 in CD8+ T cell dysfunction regulation and propose an immune regulatory axis, H3K9la/IL-11/JAK2/STAT3, that drives tumor development and immune escape in HNSCC. Blocking the IL-11-mediated crosstalk between tumor and CD8+ T cells restore the killing function of the latter and enhances immunotherapy efficiency, providing a strategy for combination immunotherapy for patients with HNSCC.

### Limitations of the study

Our study reveals that the increase in H3K9la in tumor cells promotes CD8+ T cell exhaustion via IL-11 secretion and subsequent JAK2/STAT3 activation, which leads to poor immunotherapy response in HNSCC. However, additional histone lactylation sites and other non-histone lactylation modification should be investigated to comprehend the complicated immune escape network in HNSCC. Furthermore, downstream targets of histone lactylation, not just IL-11, need to be explored, which might reveal more promising targets. The anti-IL-11 monoclonal antibody, 9MW3811 injection, was approved by the Australian Therapeutic Products Administration in February 2023, with indications for advanced malignant tumors and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. However, it is not available to us, restricting its application in our study.

### Experimental model and study participant details

#### Cell lines

We used the HNSCC following cell lines, which were purchased from the Type Culture Collection of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (Shanghai, China): CAL27, HN30, and the murine SCC cell line SCCVII. Jurkat were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (Manassas, VA, USA).

#### Mice

The animal experiments performed here were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of the Ninth People’s Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine. C3H/He mice (4–6 weeks of age) were purchased from Shanghai Laboratory Animal Center (Shanghai, China). All animal studies were performed in accordance with the Guide for Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (The Ministry of Science and Technology of China, 2006).

### Method details

#### Clinical specimens

From 2018 to 2019, 138 HNSCC tumor tissue specimens and 84 normal adjacent tissues were collected at the Ninth People’s Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine. The tissues were embedded and constructed a tissue microarray. A randomized controlled phase II clinical study of carelizumab combined with chemotherapy in the perioperative treatment of locally advanced primary HNSCC (Camoral project, registration No: ChiCTR2000037980) was still ongoing in our institution. The responders and non-responders after adjuvant immunotherapy were enrolled in this study. Informed consent was obtained from all patients. This study was approved by Ethics Committee of Shanghai Ninth People’s Hospital affiliated Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine. Written informed consents were received from all patients.

#### Cell lines and cell culture

The cancer cells were cultured in DMEM (Gibco, MA, USA), while Jurkat cells were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium (Gibco). The culture medium was supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco) before use. The cell cultures were maintained at 37°C in a 5% CO 2 environment.

#### RNA extraction and quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis

The total RNA was extracted using the TRIzol reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), and qRT-PCR was performed using the StepOnePlus real-time quantitative PCR system (Applied Biosystems, MA, USA). The primer sequences used here are listed in [Table S1](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#mmc1).

#### RNA interference and viral transfection

Following the manufacturer’s instructions, RNAiMAX was used for the siRNA transfection of cells, and Lipofectamine 3000 and P3000 were used for plasmid transfection. The siRNA and lentiviral constructs used here were purchased from Genomeditech (Shanghai, China). To establish a stable transfected SCCVII cell line, puromycin (2.5 μg/mL) was used for selection for seven days. The siRNA sequences are listed in [Table S1](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#mmc1).

#### Immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence assays

After deparaffinization, rehydration and antigen retrieval, slides were incubated with primary antibody at 4°C.[40](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#)

The staining evaluation score was calculated by multiplying the staining intensity by the percentage of positive cells. #### Multiple immunofluorescence assay

Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded specimens were subjected to sequential immunostaining. The tissues were incubated with primary antibodies overnight and then with secondary antibodies for 1 h at a temperature range 20°C–26°C, followed by a microwave treatment and re-staining with the primary antibodies. The following antibodies were used: anti-CD8 rabbit antibody against SCCVII tumors (ab209775, Abcam, MA, USA), anti-PD1 rabbit antibody (66220-1-Ig, Proteintech Group, IL, USA), and the nuclear dye DAPI (D21490, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The antibodies used in the tissue microarray multicolor fluorescence analysis included those against pan-Kla, H3K9la (PTM-1401RM, PTM-1419RM, PTM Bio, China), pan cytokeratin (panCK) (4545S, Cell Signaling Technology, MA, USA), PD1 (66220-1-Ig, Proteintech Group), and CD8 (85336S, Cell Signaling Technology).

#### Flow cytometry assay

For the tumor infiltration lymphocyte staining assays, the cell samples were incubated with specific antibodies for surface markers and intracellular markers. For mouse samples, the antibodies used included anti-mouse CD45 Percp-cy5.5 (103132), anti-mouse CD3 APC-cy7 (100222), anti-mouse CD8 BV650 (100742), and anti-mouse PD1 PE-cyanine 7 (135216), and intracellular antibodies, including anti-mouse granzyme B PE (372208), anti-mouse interferon gamma APC (505810), and anti-mouse Ki67 BV605 (652413), under light-proof conditions. For human CD8+ T cell analysis, anti-human CD152 APC (349908), anti-human TIGIT BV421 (372710), anti-human CD366 PE-cyanine 7 (345013), and anti-human CD279 PE (379210) were used for flow cytometric staining. The above antibodies were purchased from Biolegend (CA, USA). Carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester (CFSE, 65-0850-84, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used in the CD8+ T cell experiments mentioned. All antibodies against immune cells were purchased from PeproTech (NJ, USA) and the results were analyzed using a BD Fortessa cytometer (BD Biosciences).

#### CUT&Tag

Following the manufacturer’s instructions of the CUT&Tag kit used (cat#53170, Active motif, CA, USA), a hyperactive _in-situ_ ChIP Library Prep Kit for Illumina (pG-Tn5) (TD901, Vazyme Biotech, China) was used for the CUT&Tag assay. Briefly, after the experimental treatment, cells were collected and bound to concanavalin A beads. The cells were then incubated with an anti-H3K9la primary antibody (PTM-1419RM; PTM Bio), followed by incubation with the secondary antibodies. pA-Tn5 transposase was combined with the processed samples. After activation of Tn5 transposase-mediated transposition, the DNA was extracted and amplified to construct a DNA library. VAHTS DNA Clean beads (N411; Vazyme Biotech) were used for DNA purification. The library was quantified using the VAHTS Library Quantification Kit for Illumina (Vazyme Biotech), and library sequencing was conducted using the Illumina NovaSeq 150 PE platform. Data was analyzed by Genefund Biotech (Shanghai, China).

#### RNA-seq

Total RNA was extracted from CAL27 and HN30 cells using TRIzol reagent (10296010, Thermo Fisher Scientific) after treating them with 20 mM lactate for 24 h. Sequencing libraries were prepared as previously described.[41](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(24)01037-4#)

#### Measurement of the lactate levels

Following the manufacturer’s protocol, the cell supernatant was processed using a lactate quantification kit (A01921, NJJCBIO, Nanjin, China). The lactate concentration was then measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay plate reader (Synergy H1, Agilent BioTek, CA, USA) at a reference wavelength of 530 nm.

#### Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)

To determine the concentration of IL11 in the cell culture supernatant, an ELISA was performed using an IL11 ELISA kit (D1100, R&D, MN, USA) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions.

#### Human CD8+ T cell isolation

A human CD8 MicroBeads kit (130-045-201; Miltenyi Biotec, CA, USA) was used to isolate human CD8+ T cells from the peripheral blood of healthy controls. The experiments were performed according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. Sorted cells were stimulated with 2 μg/mL anti-human CD3 antibody (01121-25, BioGems, CA, USA) overnight, and then with anti-human CD28 antibody (10311-25, BioGems) and recombinant human IL2 (200-02, PeproTech, NJ, USA) for 48 h. Then, stimulated cells were transferred into a new dish containing fresh RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1% glutamine, and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco).

#### Animal study

For the subcutaneous implantation model, 1 × 10 5 SCCVII cells were injected into the flanks of mice, with or without the indicated treatments. The length (L)and width (W)of the tumors were measured every two or three days from the 15 th day after injection onwards, and the volume was calculated as L×W 2×π/6. ## **Webpage Content** 
Title: Integrative network modeling reveals mechanisms underlying T cell exhaustion

URL Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8

Markdown Content:
## Introduction

Diverse mechanisms can limit T cell responses to tumors and immunotherapies[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR1 "Thommen, D. S. & Schumacher, T. N. T cell dysfunction in cancer. Cancer Cell 33, 547–562 (2018).") (summarized in Supplementary Fig.[S1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)). In particular, CD8+ T cells stimulated without the appropriate co-stimulatory signals can become anergic, while telomere erosion and/or DNA damage can result in T cell senescence[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR2 "Wherry, E. J. & Kurachi, M. Molecular and cellular insights into T cell exhaustion. Nat. Rev. Immunol. 15, 486–499 (2015).") over periods spanning months/years. T cell exhaustion (TCE) occurs in spite of physiologically appropriate stimulation when stimulation is prolonged to periods of weeks[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR2 "Wherry, E. J. & Kurachi, M. Molecular and cellular insights into T cell exhaustion. Nat. Rev. Immunol. 15, 486–499 (2015)."), as is often the case for tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and engineered T cells. TCE is defined by high expression of inhibitory receptors, and lowered capacity for proliferation, cytokine production, cytotoxic activity, and memory formation[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR2 "Wherry, E. J. & Kurachi, M. Molecular and cellular insights into T cell exhaustion. Nat. Rev. Immunol. 15, 486–499 (2015)."). To date, immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting inhibitory receptors and other immunotherapies have shown great success in only subsets of patients across multiple cancers[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR3 "Marin-Acevedo, J. A., Soyano, A. E., Dholaria, B., Knutson, K. L. & Lou, Y. Cancer immunotherapy beyond immune checkpoint inhibitors. J. Hematol. Oncol. 11, 8 (2018)."). The limited efficacy of checkpoint inhibitors and their adverse effects in some patients[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR4 "Hassel, J. C. et al. Combined immune checkpoint blockade (anti-PD-1/anti-CTLA-4): evaluation and management of adverse drug reactions. Cancer Treat. Rev. 57, 36–49 (2017)."),[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR5 "Bonifant, C. L., Jackson, H. J., Brentjens, R. J. & Curran, K. J. Toxicity and management in CAR T-cell therapy. Mol. Ther. Oncolytics 3, 16011 (2016).") suggest a need for a better understanding of TCE and the development of new TCE inhibitors. A better understanding of the mechanisms underlying TCE may improve the efficacy and reduce the adverse effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR), engineered T cell receptor (TCR), and T cell engager immunotherapies[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR3 "Marin-Acevedo, J. A., Soyano, A. E., Dholaria, B., Knutson, K. L. & Lou, Y. Cancer immunotherapy beyond immune checkpoint inhibitors. J. Hematol. Oncol. 11, 8 (2018).").

In response to acute infections, naïve and memory CD8+ T cells both undergo a stereotyped series of transcriptional state changes, summarized in Fig.[1a](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig1). CD8+ T cells receiving prolonged stimulation by chronic infections or cancer antigens undergo a qualitatively similar set of state changes (Fig.[1b](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig1)), but become increasingly exhausted over time.

**Figure 1**

Multiple cellular state transitions underlie CD8+ T cell responses to acute and chronic co-stimulation. (**a**) Literature-based model of the acute response. CD8+ T cell activation starts with a complex and highly regulated process of antigen sampling (brief cell-cell contacts) that minimizes the risk of a response to self-antigens while sensitively detecting matching non-self antigens. Identification of a target cell results in the formation of a stable immune synapse and the activation of the T cell receptor (TCR) and its associated co-receptors (known as signals 2 and 3). TCR co-stimulation in turn leads to rapid and robust T cell proliferation. The magnitude of T cell amplification is controlled via a FAS/FASL mediated apoptotic signaling process known as restimulation-induced cell death (RICD). Activated CD8+ T cells differentiate into memory precursor and short-lived effector cells. Effector cells require cytokines such as IL2 for survival, and undergo cell death when antigen clearance leads to loss of cytokine signaling, a process known as cytokine withdrawal-induced cell death (CWID). After antigen clearance, memory CD8+ T cells are formed from the pro-memory/proliferative (PP) population in a process that takes several weeks. (**b**) In response to chronic co-stimulation, CD8+ T cells undergo state changes similar to (**a**). Prolonged activation reduces the proportion of memory-precursor cells, while persistence of cytokine signaling antagonizes CWID and leads to a hypo-functional effector/exhausted state.

Importantly, the early stages of T cell activation and exhaustion are not steady states (i.e. self-maintaining), but require continued stimulation by antigen and associated co-stimulatory signals (hereinafter referred to as Ag for brevity). Prolonged stimulation eventually drives T cells into irreversible (steady state) exhaustion, maintained by epigenetic changes[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR6 "Ghoneim, H. E., Zamora, A. E., Thomas, P. G. & Youngblood, B. A. Cell-intrinsic barriers of T cell-based immunotherapy. Trends Mol. Med. 22, 1000–1011 (2016)."). How a single regulatory input (Ag presence/absence) can reliably drive the multiple transitory state changes that occur during prolonged stimulation (Fig.[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig1)) is currently poorly understood.

In recent years, a number of groundbreaking studies have identified key regulatory genes and interactions underlying CD8+ TCE[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR7 "Singer, M. et al. A distinct gene module for dysfunction uncoupled from activation in tumor-infiltrating T cells. Cell 166, 1500–1511.e9 (2016)."),[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR8 "Zheng, C. et al. Landscape of infiltrating T cells in liver cancer revealed by single-cell sequencing. Cell 169, 1342–1356.e16 (2017)."),[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR9 "Philip, M. et al. Chromatin states define tumour-specific T cell dysfunction and reprogramming. Nature 545, 452–456 (2017)."),[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR10 "Im, S. J. et al. Defining CD8+ T cells that provide the proliferative burst after PD-1 therapy. Nature 537, 417–421 (2016)."),[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR11 "He, R. et al. Follicular CXCR5-expressing CD8+ T cells curtail chronic viral infection. Nature 537, 412–428 (2016)."),[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR12 "Leong, Y. A. et al. CXCR5+ follicular cytotoxic T cells control viral infection in B cell follicles. Nat. Immunol. 17, 1187–1196 (2016)."). In spite of the differences in model systems and experimental protocols, these studies reveal a common set of regulatory interactions underlying TCE. However, all known genes and gene products whose expression or modification state have been associated with TCE also play a role in normal (acute) T cell activation[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR13 "Fuertes Marraco, S. A., Neubert, N. J., Verdeil, G. & Speiser, D. E. Inhibitory receptors beyond T cell exhaustion. Front. Immunol. 6, 310 (2015)."). We hypothesized that TCE may arise from changes in diverse gene regulatory interactions rather than the dysregulation of a single gene.

Here, we present a manually curated, literature-based, and data-driven network of gene regulatory interactions underpinning TCE in CD8+ cells. Using diverse published data, we show that the TCE network accurately captures the gene expression states of CD8+ T cells in both chronic infection and tumor settings.

Analysis of functionally distinct network motifs reveals multiple overlapping interactions, implementing overlying sets of functional modules (system building blocks) that appear to reinforce each other’s function, and lead to robust, highly stereotypic cellular state changes following activation. A simple mathematical model derived from the network’s functional modules suggests exhaustion arises because the duration of time that activated CD8+ T cells spend in a memory-progenitor state is independent of the duration of stimulation, whereas differentiation is prolonged with stimulation. We use our 2-state TCE network model to predict the phenotypic effects of targeted drugs and provide experimental evidence in support of this approach.

## Results

We initially used manual curation of the literature to establish a network of key molecular interactions that are believed to underlie TCE (Supplementary Table[S1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1) and Supplementary Fig.[S2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)). We then superimposed onto this network expression levels of each gene at various stages of T cell activation and exhaustion from published datasets (see Methods; example visualizations shown in Supplementary Figs. S3–8.

Next, we calculated fold changes in expression compared to the naïve state and evaluated the fraction of times each interaction exhibited fold changes in source and target genes consistent with the reported sense of the interaction (promoting or inhibitory). At a false discovery rate of ~15% (estimated via permutation testing), only 17 interactions (~3.6%) in the network did not have supportive expression data (see Methods and Supplementary Fig.[S9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)).

Consistent with the observation that all driver genes implicated in TCE are common to, and play similar roles in, exhausted and acute responses, principal component analysis (PCA) of expression data for the genes in the TCE network exhibited similar trajectories for acute and exhausted gene expression profiles. TCE gene sets from previous studies also showed similar trajectories and further support our findings (Supplementary Fig.[S10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)).

In addition to known regulators of TCR stimulation and co-receptor engagement, T cells subjected to repeat stimulation and exhaustion undergo multiple metabolic changes[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR14 "McKinney, E. F. & Smith, K. G. C. Metabolic exhaustion in infection, cancer and autoimmunity. Nat. Immunol. 19, 213–221 (2018)."),[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR15 "Buck, M. D., Sowell, R. T., Kaech, S. M. & Pearce, E. L. Metabolic instruction of immunity. Cell 169, 570–586 (2017)."). Indeed, metabolic deprivation can ameliorate T cell activation[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR16 "Kornberg, M. D. et al. Dimethyl fumarate targets GAPDH and aerobic glycolysis to modulate immunity. Science 360, 449–453 (2018)."). Consistent with our TCE network findings, analysis of gene expression changes driving metabolic switching during acute and chronic stimulation also suggested similar expression state trajectories for CD8+ cells undergoing acute and chronic stimulation (Supplementary Figs.[S11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1) and [S12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)).

Considering that the genes involved in both acute and chronic stimulation are largely the same (as revealed by the literature-based network), and that the trajectories of their expression changes are also similar (as revealed by our gene expression and metabolic analyses), we hypothesized that the differences between acute and chronic T cell responses may lie in the timing of gene expression changes.

To find differences in the relative timing of gene expression changes between acute and chronic responses, we carried out time course gene expression clustering (Supplementary Figs. S13–15) and looked for transcription factors and signaling genes that switch cluster membership (i.e. timing) between acute and chronic settings. This approach identified metabolic changes downstream of _TP53_ as differentially regulated in acute and chronic settings. Of the three _TP53_ regulatory genes whose expression changes correlated with the TCE network genes, only one gene (CD200-R1, a known T cell suppressor[17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR17 "Misstear, K. et al. Suppression of antigen-specific T cell responses by the Kaposi’s sarcoma-associated herpesvirus viral OX2 protein and its cellular orthologue, CD200. J. Virol. 86, 6246–6257 (2012)."),[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR18 "Rosenblum, M. D. et al. CD200 is a novel p53-target gene involved in apoptosis-associated immune tolerance. Blood 103, 2691–2698 (2004)."),[19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR19 "Rijkers, E. S. et al. The inhibitory CD200R is differentially expressed on human and mouse T and B lymphocytes. Mol. Immunol. 45, 1126–1135 (2008).")) showed consistently large fold change differences between chronic and acute settings in multiple datasets (Supplementary Fig.[S16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)). However, recent research suggests CD200-R1 activity inhibits T cell responses primarily through CD8+ T cell independent pathways[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR20 "Zemans, R. L. Neutrophil-mediated T-cell suppression in influenza: novel finding raising additional questions. Am. J. Respir. Cell Mol. Biol. 58, 423–425 (2018)."),[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR21 "Caserta, S. et al. Chronic infection drives expression of the inhibitory receptor CD200R, and its ligand CD200, by mouse and human CD4 T cells. PLoS One 7, e35466 (2012)."),[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR22 "Rygiel, T. P. et al. Lack of CD200 enhances pathological T cell responses during influenza infection. J. Immunol. 183, 1990–1996 (2009).").

### Network analysis

In contrast to the above findings, a series of alternate logic models of the TCE network (see Methods) all required specific gene activation delays in order to recapitulate the observed sequences of CD8+ cell gene expression changes during acute and chronic stimulation (Supplementary Figs. S17–20 and Methods for examples). Feed forward and feedback loops (Supplementary Fig.[S21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)) are widely used to control timing and activity in both biological and engineered systems[23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR23 "Alon, U. An Introduction to Systems Biology: Design Principles of Biological Circuits (Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, FL, 2006)."),[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR24 "Bolouri, H. Computational Modeling of Gene Regulatory Networks – a Primer (Imperial College Press, London, 2008)."). Thus, to address how antigen availability can determine a sequence of specifically timed gene expression changes, we searched for feed-forward and feedback motifs in our literature-derived TCE network.

To facilitate loop detection, the initial literature-based TCE network was simplified by collapsing all isoforms of each gene into a single gene symbol (e.g. _NF-κB_ instead of _RELB_, _cREL_, etc.) unless a specific isoform was known to play a distinct role in TCE. Similarly, chains of interactions with no incoming or outgoing branches were collapsed into single nodes, and (where possible), members of protein complexes were grouped into single nodes. Finally, genes with no reported downstream targets and unknown regulatory significance were removed. To maximize loop detection, we then carried out a second, more detailed literature review to identify all known interactions of the genes in our reduced literature-based TCE network. The resulting network has 64 nodes and 120 interactions (Supplementary Fig.[S22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1) and Supplementary Table[S2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)).

### Genes in the TCE network can be divided into early and late activity classes

Multiple recent studies of TCE have noted the existence of distinct ‘reversible’ and ‘irreversible’ subpopulations of exhausted CD8+ T cells[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR10 "Im, S. J. et al. Defining CD8+ T cells that provide the proliferative burst after PD-1 therapy. Nature 537, 417–421 (2016)."),[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR11 "He, R. et al. Follicular CXCR5-expressing CD8+ T cells curtail chronic viral infection. Nature 537, 412–428 (2016)."),[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR12 "Leong, Y. A. et al. CXCR5+ follicular cytotoxic T cells control viral infection in B cell follicles. Nat. Immunol. 17, 1187–1196 (2016)."). Reversibly exhausted CD8+ T cells have been variously defined by high expression levels of _CXCR5_, _TCF-1_, and _BCL6_, and concurrent low expression of _KLRG1_, _BLIMP-1 (PRDM1)_, and _TIM3 (HAVCR2)_[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR25 "Wang, C., Singer, M. & Anderson, A. C. Molecular dissection of CD8+ T-cell dysfunction. Trends Immunol. 38, 567–576 (2017)."). They have relatively high proliferative potential and can produce fully functional memory cells[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR25 "Wang, C., Singer, M. & Anderson, A. C. Molecular dissection of CD8+ T-cell dysfunction. Trends Immunol. 38, 567–576 (2017)."). In contrast, irreversibly exhausted CD8+ T cells are defined by the opposite expression pattern and have low proliferative and memory-forming potential.

While performing expression clustering and time course analysis of the TCE network genes, we noticed that markers of ‘reversible exhaustion’ (e.g. high _CXCR5_ in LCMV infections, high _TCF-1_ in tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, accompanied with low levels of _KLRG1_ and _TIM-3_) overlap with and include pro-memory genes, and exclude genes associated with effector function and ‘irreversible exhaustion’ (Supplementary Fig.[S23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)). Moreover, many genes associated with the reversible exhaustion state are also associated with proliferation (notably _TCF-1, MYC, NF-κB_, and genes enabling glycolysis). These findings led us to hypothesize that the processes underlying CD8+ T cell activation and exhaustion may fall into 2 broad classes: pro-memory and proliferative(PP), versus pro-effector and exhaustion.

Using clustered gene expression time course profiles (Supplementary Figs. S13–15) and consistent with literature reports, we were able to assign the regulatory interactions underlying TCE into 2 groups defining an early, PP, and a later state associated with effector differentiation and function ultimately leading to irreversible exhaustion (EE). The resulting network model is illustrated in Fig.[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig2). It is important to note that in terms of nodes (i.e. genes/gene products) and interactions, the network in Fig.[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig2) is identical to that in Supplementary Fig.[S22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1) (i.e. both are visualizations of the citations listed in Supplementary Table[S2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)). The key differences are that the layout and coloring of the network have been manually adjusted to highlight the PP and EE network components and their interactions.

Nodes on a green background represent molecules and processes associated with the late effector/irreversibly exhausted (EE) state. ### Network motifs identify modular functional building blocks

We next used the 2-state TCE network of Fig.[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig2) to search for regulatory network motifs and functional building blocks that may explain the state changes of CD8+ cells undergoing TCE. A summary of the functional network motifs/building blocks discovered is presented in Fig.[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig3) and Supplementary Fig.[S24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1).

#### Mutual inhibition between early and late activation states

Excluding the negative-feedback interactions of the inhibitory receptors, a remarkable 18 out of 23 inhibitory interactions in our TCE network (78%) are between ‘early’ (PP) and ‘late’ (EE) activation genes (Fig.[3a](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig3) and Supplementary Fig.[S24a](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)). Such inhibition can enable the mutual exclusion of these 2 essential activation states in either a graded or bistable manner[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR24 "Bolouri, H. Computational Modeling of Gene Regulatory Networks – a Primer (Imperial College Press, London, 2008)."). Consistent with this hypothesis, recently published single-cell RNA-seq data[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR8 "Zheng, C. et al. Landscape of infiltrating T cells in liver cancer revealed by single-cell sequencing. Cell 169, 1342–1356.e16 (2017).") suggest _BCL6_ and _BLIMP-1_ repress each other in a mutually exclusive manner (Supplementary Fig.[S25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)).

#### Overlapping incoherent feed-forward loops fix the duration of the pro-memory PP state

In an incoherent feed forward loop (iFFL), an upstream regulator activates and represses a downstream target via pathways that operate on different timescales[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR26 "Goentoro, L., Shoval, O., Kirschner, M. W. & Alon, U. The incoherent feedforward loop can provide fold-change detection in gene regulation. Mol. Cell 36, 894–899 (2009)."). One characteristic behavior of such regulation is that the downstream target will be turned on (or off) for a fixed duration corresponding to the difference in the timescales of the activating and inhibitory pathways.

As summarized in Fig.[3b](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig3) and Supplementary Fig.[S24b](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1), a set of overlapping iFFLs ensure delayed loss of nuclear FOXO1 protein activity, and concomitant loss of _TCF-1_ gene expression. FOXO1 and TCF-1 are both expressed in naïve and memory T cells[27](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR27 "Hess Michelini, R., Doedens, A. L., Goldrath, A. W. & Hedrick, S. M. Differentiation of CD8 memory T cells depends on Foxo1. J. Exp. Med. 210, 1189–1200 (2013)."),[28](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR28 "Delpoux, A., Lai, C. Y., Hedrick, S. M. & Doedens, A. L. FOXO1 opposition of CD8+ T cell effector programming confers early memory properties and phenotypic diversity. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 114, E8865–E8874 (2017)."). Following T cell stimulation, their expression is abrogated by delayed Polycomb repressor complex 2 (PRC2)-mediated inhibition downstream of TCR signaling (see also Supplementary Table[S3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1))[29](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR29 "Gray, S. M., Amezquita, R. A., Guan, T., Kleinstein, S. H. & Kaech, S. M. Polycomb repressive complex 2-mediated chromatin repression guides effector CD8+ T cell terminal differentiation and loss of multipotency. Immunity 46, 596–608 (2017)."),[30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR30 "Kakaradov, B. et al. Early transcriptional and epigenetic regulation of CD8+ T cell differentiation revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing. Nat. Immunol. 18, 422–432 (2017)."). An additional set of iFFLs involving repression of FOXO1 by signaling downstream of the IL2 and IL12 receptors further reinforces delayed repression of TCF-1. Taking these observations together, we hypothesize that the duration of _FOXO1/TCF-1_ transcription following stimulation is fixed by the time it takes for TCR-activated PRC2 and signaling pathways to silence the 2 genes. The sequences of early and late regulatory interactions governing _TCF-1_ expression are illustrated schematically in Fig.[4a,b](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig4).

Focusing on interactions among the ‘early’ genes and cell surface receptors in the TCE network revealed an additional iFFL that regulates the timing of FAS/FASL signaling (Fig.[3b](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig3) and Supplementary Fig.[S24b](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)). Viral IFN-regulatory factors inhibit activation-induced cell death via two positive regulatory IFN-regulatory factor 1-dependent domains in the CD95 ligand promoter. J. Immunol. 168, 1226–1234 (2002)."), is repressed early on by BACH2[32](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR32 "Roychoudhuri, R. et al. BACH2 regulates CD8+ T cell differentiation by controlling access of AP-1 factors to enhancers. Nat. Immunol. 17, 851–860 (2016)."), which is expressed in naïve CD8+ T cells[33](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR33 "Tsukumo, S. et al. BACH2 maintains T cells in a naive state by suppressing effector memory-related genes. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 110, 10735–10740 (2013).") and activated by TCR-mediated signaling (Fig.[4c](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig4)). At later time points, TCR-activated PRC2 epigenetically represses _BACH2_ expression[29](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR29 "Gray, S. M., Amezquita, R. A., Guan, T., Kleinstein, S. H. & Kaech, S. M. Polycomb repressive complex 2-mediated chromatin repression guides effector CD8+ T cell terminal differentiation and loss of multipotency. Immunity 46, 596–608 (2017)."), thus enabling FAS/FASL activation by IFN-γ (Fig.[4d](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig4)).

A third set of overlapping iFFLs ensure the delayed activation of the late/effector state genes _TBET_, _ZEB2_, and _BLIMP-1_ (Fig.[3b](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig3) and Supplementary Fig.[S24b](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)). Thus, the duration of activity of early/progenitor state (PP) genes, the timing of the activation of the late effector/exhausted state (EE) genes, and the timing of FAS/FASL signaling to limit proliferation, are all controlled by overlapping iFFLs that share many genes and reinforce each other’s function in a coordinated, redundantly robust manner.

With the exception of _TCF-1/BCL6_ mutual activation, the regulatory interactions of the early-phase genes in the TCE network are mediated entirely by iFFLs. We hypothesize that these iFFLs create a fixed duration time window during which activated T cells proliferate, are in a memory precursor state, and are capable of reinvigoration.

#### Negative feedback by inhibitory receptors

Negative feedback (Supplementary Fig.[S21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1) and Fig.[3c](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig3) and Supplementary Fig.[S24c](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)) is a well described mechanism for homeostasis. At least 2 distinct sets of negative feedbacks appear to regulate TCE. Firstly, negative feedback via FAS/FASL signaling results in restimulation-induced cell death[34](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR34 "Snow, A. L., Pandiyan, P., Zheng, L., Krummey, S. M. & Lenardo, M. J. The power and the promise of restimulation-induced cell death in human immune diseases. Immunol. Rev. 236, 68–82 (2010).") (RICD, Fig.[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig1)) and is thought to limit T cell numbers following activation-induced proliferation[34](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR34 "Snow, A. L., Pandiyan, P., Zheng, L., Krummey, S. M. & Lenardo, M. J. The power and the promise of restimulation-induced cell death in human immune diseases. Immunol. Rev. 236, 68–82 (2010).").

In addition, and in contrast to population control via FAS-mediated RICD, negative feedback via inhibitory receptors primarily acts by down-regulating signal transduction downstream of the TCR[35](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR35 "Hannier, S., Tournier, M., Bismuth, G. & Triebel, F. CD3/TCR complex-associated lymphocyte activation gene-3 molecules inhibit CD3/TCR signaling. J. Immunol. 161, 4058–4065 (1998)."),[36](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR36 "Anderson, A. C., Joller, N. & Kuchroo, V. K. Lag-3, Tim-3, and TIGIT: co-inhibitory receptors with specialized functions in immune regulation. #### Positive feedback loops maintain the late EE state

In contrast to the early PP state, the later EE state has no iFFLs and is instead self-reinforced via multiple positive feedback loops (Fig.[3d](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig3) and Supplementary Fig.[S24d](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)). Importantly, such feedback loops stabilize the expression of not only the nodes directly involved in each loop (NFATC1, IRF4, TBET, ZEB2, and BLIMP-1), but also their regulatory targets, which include CTLA4, PD-1, TIM3, LAG3, IFN-γ, GZMA/B, PRF1, FAS/FASL, 2B4, CD160, and TIGIT.

### Known interactions are sufficient to explain T cell exhaustion

As noted above (Figs.[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig3) and [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig4), and Supplementary Fig.[S24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#MOESM1)), the onset of the late EE state leads to the repression of key drivers of the early PP state. Moreover, the transition between the 2 states occurs at a fixed time post-stimulation dictated by delayed/slow regulatory interactions within iFFLs, and independent of the duration of stimulation. Thus, the longer that T cell stimulation continues, the more time a given CD8+ T cell will spend reinforcing its EE state at the cost of pro-memory and proliferative states. Figure[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig5) presents simulation results illustrating this principle (see Methods for details).

### The 2-state TCE model allows prediction of drug effects

To identify optimal targets for counteracting exhaustion, we first computed all downstream targets of each gene in the TCE network (see Methods for details). Depending on whether an interaction is inhibitory or activating, lowered activity of an upstream regulator will increase or decrease the activity of target genes. To estimate the overall phenotypic effect of an upstream gene, we calculated a pro-PP score by adding the number of up-regulated PP genes to the number of down-regulated EE genes, and a complementary pro-EE score.

As shown in Fig.[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig6), blocking or reducing the activity of most genes in the TCE network results in exclusively pro-PP or pro-EE predicted effects. A small number of genes appear to impact both PP and EE states because they play distinct pro-PP or pro-EE roles at different times post-stimulation. For example, transcription of _EZH2_ (that expresses the core subunit of PRC2) is up-regulated following TCR co-stimulation, peaks at ~1 day post-infection, and is largely back to basal levels by day 7 post-infection[30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR30 "Kakaradov, B. et al. Early transcriptional and epigenetic regulation of CD8+ T cell differentiation revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing. Nat. Immunol. 18, 422–432 (2017)."). At the protein level, PRC2 activity peaks around 3–5 days post-infection[41](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR41 "He, S. et al. Ezh2 phosphorylation state determines its capacity to maintain CD8+ T memory precursors for antitumor immunity. Nat. Commun. 8, 2125 (2017)."),[42](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR42 "Youngblood, B. et al. Effector CD8 T cells dedifferentiate into long-lived memory cells. Nature 552, 404–409 (2017)."), at which time EZH2/PRC2 suppress the already active pro-memory/proliferation genes _FOXO1_ and _TCF-1_ while suppressing the pro-effector/exhaustion gene _EOMES_ (Figs.[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig6) and [7a–c](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig7)). Thus, based on the network topology alone, it appears as though EZH2 represses both the PP and EE network states, but time step analysis resolves the apparent contradiction and suggests reduction of EZH2 activity should have exclusively pro-PP effects (because EZH2 is inactive at the times when it could have pro-EE effects).

## Discussion

The network analysis presented here suggests CD8+ TCE arises from an inherent topological property of the network of regulatory interactions that underlie CD8+ T cell responses to both acute and prolonged stimulation. Specifically, we presented computational and experimental evidence suggesting that the duration of time CD8+ T cells spend in a pro-memory state is fixed by network properties that limit the duration of activity of the pro-memory gene _TCF-1_ in a manner independent of the duration of stimulation.

A recently published study used mass cytometry to classify exhausted CD8+ T cells into multiple subtypes[43](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR43 "Bengsch, B. et al. Epigenomic-guided mass cytometry profiling reveals disease-specific features of exhausted CD8 T cells. Immunity 48, 1029–1045.e5 (2018)."). Consistent with our model, Bengsch _et al_.[43](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR43 "Bengsch, B. et al. Epigenomic-guided mass cytometry profiling reveals disease-specific features of exhausted CD8 T cells. Immunity 48, 1029–1045.e5 (2018).") report that in HIV infections with a lower viral load and in HIV patients on anti-retroviral therapy (i.e. cases with greater immune activity), exhausted T cells have higher expression levels of TCF-1 and/or CXCR5 and appear more functional. Further supporting our model, drug-induced activation of TCF-1 has been shown to block CD8+ T cell differentiation and increase proliferation[44](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR44 "Gattinoni, L. et al. Wnt signaling arrests effector T cell differentiation and generates CD8+ memory stem cells. Nat. Med. 15, 808–813 (2009).").

The analyses presented here focused on molecules and interactions generally accepted by the research community to play important roles in CD8+ T cell responses to acute and chronic stimulation. It is important to note that the approach presented here can be easily extended to predict novel molecules and interactions by extending our literature-based network to include known and predicted protein-protein and protein-DNA interactors of the current network nodes.

Analysis of our literature-based, data-driven, and manually curated TCE network suggests TCE is a highly robust process mediated by multiple redundant and overlapping feedback and feed-forward loops. In addition, diverse, overlapping molecular mechanisms contribute to TCE, including combinatorial regulation by transcription factors, post-translational modifications, protein localization, chromatin state changes, and metabolic reprogramming. Taken together, our analyses are consistent with the view that TCE is not a dysfunctional state, but rather an adaptive response to situations where the immune system fails to clear antigen rapidly. Clinical remediation of TCE will need to overcome multiple, overlapping and redundant regulatory mechanisms, requiring combinatorial interventions.

### Construction of the literature-based TCE network

The large-scale network of regulatory interactions underlying CD8+ TCE was manually curated from reports in publications released before August 2017, focusing on genes reported by multiple publications, as well as genes with small-scale (non-‘omics’) experimental support in a single paper. For brevity, only key publications are cited. In situations where different transcripts or protein isoforms may be involved, all isoforms were included with a view to evaluating them using expression data.

The 64-node reduced/simplified TCE network was extracted and curated manually by one co-author, and then independently verified on an interaction-by-interaction and citation-by-citation level by a second co-author.

### Network visualization

Both the large-scale TCE network, and its simplified version were visualized using the RCyjs ([http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/RCyjs.html](http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/RCyjs.html)).

Expression data were superimposed onto the large-scale TCE network using Rcyjs. Fold changes were calculated with respect to naïve CD8+ T cells and mapped to a color-scale as shown. Edge (line) thicknesses are proportional to the fraction of observations in which the source and target genes in an edge have fold changes concordant with the sense of the interaction (‘promoting’ or ‘inhibiting’). Thus, the auto-regulatory loop of NFATC1 – by definition – has maximum thickness. In some instances, edges were highly concordant (good agreement between the network model and data) in one dataset or condition, and not in another.

### Network evaluation by concordance matching

For each edge (interaction) in the TCE network, the fraction of times when the source and target genes in an edge had fold changes concordant with the sense of the interaction (‘promoting’ or ‘inhibiting’) were calculated. To account for variability in the data, fold changes were calculated _per replicate_ data (instead of averaging data across all replicates). Thus, data for 2 replicates across 2 conditions generated 4 possible comparisons with potential average concordance values of (0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00).

To explore the statistical significance of the observed edge concordance values, 500,000 edges were generated with randomly assigned gene labels and interaction types. Next, the fraction of times an edge was concordant in a given dataset for the TCE and randomized (control) networks was calculated. Concordant edges occurred by chance in 14.8% of randomized controls, suggesting a false discovery rate of ~15%.

### State tracking by PCA

To compare the TCE network state changes among different CD8+ T cell subsets, PCA was performed for each dataset using the normalized expression levels of all the genes in the TCE network. The relative positions of any 2 CD8+ cell subtypes on a plot of the first 2 components reflect their similarities/differences in expression of the TCE network genes and show similar state trajectories for responses to acute and chronic stimulation.

### Expression cluster analysis

Expression clustering of time course data was performed using the ‘soft clustering’ method of the Bioconductor/R package ‘Mfuzz’ ([https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/Mfuzz.html](https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/Mfuzz.html))[52](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR52 "Kumar, L. & E. Futschik, M. Mfuzz: A software package for soft clustering of microarray data. Bioinformation 2, 5–7 (2007)."). Soft clustering is an unsupervised approach that allows a single gene to potentially be a member of multiple clusters. In initial explorations, the number of clusters generated by Mfuzz was varied to find the number of clusters that was large enough to result in at least 1 cluster with few members and with at least 2 clusters showing visually similar profiles. These criteria ensure that each expression cluster is tightly defined with a highly correlated set of genes while keeping the number of clusters low. Forty-nine clusters met these requirements across all datasets.

Mfuzz performs clustering on mean-centered and scaled expression profiles (Z-scores). Thus, genes are grouped by their relative change in expression, rather than absolute level of expression. In a post-processing step, we confirmed that genes of interest identified through Mfuzz clustering (e.g. CD200R1) had significant absolute expression levels and fold changes.

The above tools provide comprehensive lists of all motif occurrences, but become increasingly unwieldy for motifs with more than a handful of genes. Feed-forward and feedback loops in our network involving multiple steps (gene-gene interactions/network edges) were added manually to the list of found motifs by one author, and then independently verified by two co-authors.

### Model-based prediction of perturbation effects

To quantify the effects of knocking down the activity of individual genes in our network (e.g. via targeted drugs), we used the R package iGraph ([http://igraph.org/r/](http://igraph.org/r/)) to calculate all paths through our network model. Feedback loops that impact TCR-signaling activity (e.g. inhibitory immune receptors) were excluded from this analysis because they affect all downstream genes.

Prediction of impacts using only network topology can be misleading for genes that perform distinct functions at different times (see Fig.[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#Fig7) and related text). In particular, a target gene can appear to be both activated and repressed by an upstream regulator. For example, in naïve CD8+ T cells, ID3 represses _CXCR5_ activation by E2A. But following stimulation, ID3 activates _CXCR5_ expression. Regulatory interactions that could not be time-resolved due to lack of time course data were excluded from our analyses.

### _In vitro_ T cell cultures

Peripheral blood mononuclear cells purchased from Bloodworks Northwest (Seattle, WA) that requires informed consent from their donors. Total T cells were isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 3 human donors via negative selection (STEMCELL Technologies Inc., cat. no. 19051) and plated in anti-CD3 (BD Pharmingen clone UCHT1, cat. no. 555329) pre-coated (10 μg/ml in PBS overnight at 4 °C) 96-well round bottom plates at 100,000 cells per well in RPMI1640, 10% FBS, 0.1 mM NEAA, 1 mM Na pyruvate, 5 ng/ml anti-CD28 (eBiosciences clone CD28.2, cat no. 16-0289-85), alone or with 5 μM (reported), 0.5 μM (not shown) EZH2 inhibitor, CPI-169 (APExBio B4678) or DMSO. The same volume of EZH2 inhibitor and DMSO was added to each well to control for any DMSO effect. T cells were cultured at 37 °C, 5% CO 2. T cells were harvested on days 1, 3, 4, 8, washed in PBS and re-suspended in 350 μl RLT (Qiagen cat. no. 74136) and stored at −80 °C for future RNA isolation (Qiagen cat. no. 74136). Total T cells were also sampled and processed as other cultures on the day of isolation (day 0) and after 24 hours of incubation with 10 ng/ml human interleukin-7 (R&D Systems, cat. no. 207-IL-025) as controls for gene expression analysis. All experiments were performed according to Celgene Corporate EHS (Environmental Health and Safety) Policies and Directives.

### RNA isolation and cDNA reverse transcription

RNA was isolated from all samples using Qiagen kit (Qiagen cat. no. 74136) and quantitated on a Nanodrop 2000 spectrophotometer (ThermoScientific). 1.5 μg RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA as per protocol (Applied Biosystems cat. no. 4368814).

### Quantitative real-time PCR

qRT-PCR was performed using TaqMan Fast Advanced Master Mix (Applied Biosystems cat. no. 4444557) in a ViiA7 system (Applied Biosystems) using Applied Biosystems primers. Gene expression was quantified as per Livak & Schmittgen[62](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58600-8#ref-CR62 "Livak, K. J. & Schmittgen, T. D. Analysis of relative gene expression data using real-time quantitative PCR and the 2(-Delta Delta C(T)) method. Methods 25, 402–408 (2001).") normalized to GUSB. All measurements were performed in triplicate.

## Highlights

Naive T cell activation triggers metabolic shifts, including glycolysis and mitochondrial remodeling, supporting the transition to effector cells and their subsequent differentiation.

Metabolites from glycolysis, glutaminolysis, and the tricarboxylic acid cycle influence chromatin architecture through DNA and histone modifications, shaping T cell differentiation.

Metabolic inflexibility and mitochondrial dysfunction are central drivers of T cell dysfunction, including exhaustion, senescence, and aging, influencing transcriptional repression and epigenetic alterations.

Aging induces changes in chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and histone modifications, which affect T cell differentiation and functionality.

Understanding how metabolic stress influences epigenetic alterations in exhausted, senescent, and aged T cells is essential for developing strategies to restore immune function in aging populations.

## Abstract

CD8+ T cells are vital for antiviral and antitumor immunity, yet in hostile microenvironments, they experience metabolic stress, leading to mitochondrial damage, metabolic dysregulation, and chromatin remodeling that cause immune dysfunction. Aging further exacerbates these processes, with intrinsic metabolic collapse and extrinsic environmental factors jointly impairing T cell immunity. Metabolites orchestrate key epigenetic modifications, shaping transcriptional programs essential for T cell differentiation and memory formation. This review explores the interconnected metabolic and epigenetic mechanisms governing CD8+ T cell fate decisions, emphasizing how mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic inflexibility, and nutrient competition drive CD8+ T cell exhaustion, senescence, and age-associated dysfunction. Understanding these metabolic–epigenetic circuits offers novel therapeutic avenues, including metabolic reprogramming and senescence-targeted strategies, to rejuvenate immune responses and enhance immunotherapy outcomes.

Although stress-induced senescence shares phenotypic similarities with exhaustion, the underlying mechanisms are fundamentally distinct. ## Integration of metabolic and epigenetic signals governs T cell differentiation

Upon antigen exposure, T cells experience metabolic and epigenetic shifts to satisfy the increased energy and biosynthetic requirements necessary for effector functions and long-term survival. Effector T (Teff) cells predominantly utilize aerobic **glycolysis** (see [Glossary](https://www.cell.com/trends/endocrinology-metabolism/fulltext/S1043-2760(25)00190-0#gs0005)), **glutaminolysis**, and mitochondrial biogenesis to support rapid clonal expansion and cytokine production. ## Metabolic alteration and epigenetic regulation in aged and senescent T cells

T cells in the TME and aged individuals undergo dysfunction driven by both tumor-induced senescence and age-related metabolic decline. Though tumor-induced senescence and aging are separate processes, they converge through mitochondrial dysfunction and lipid metabolic imbalance. These shared features contribute to impaired T cell effector function, resulting in compromised antitumor immunity. The interplay between chronic metabolic stress in the TME and age-related metabolic reprogramming highlights a common pathway that drives T cell senescence and aging.

These findings underscore a converging metabolic pathway shared by tumor-induced T cell senescence and age-related decline, particularly characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and lipid dysregulation. Although senescence and aging are driven by distinct molecular programs, their metabolic convergence highlights overlapping vulnerabilities and potential therapeutic targets. Emerging studies suggest that metabolism and epigenetics are tightly interconnected in shaping T cell fate. Metabolic disturbances can alter epigenetic marks, which in turn regulate the expression of metabolic genes, thereby establishing a feedback loop that reinforces T cell dysfunction.

## Concluding remarks and future perspectives

Despite the transformative potential of immune checkpoint blockade therapies targeting PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA-4, their limited efficacy across diverse tumor types, benefiting fewer than 40% of patients, underscores the need for alternative strategies, such as epigenetic modulation, metabolic reprogramming, and combining checkpoint blockade with cytokine support [[1](https://www.cell.com/trends/endocrinology-metabolism/fulltext/S1043-2760(25)00190-0#)

]. The current limitations of the field are a call to action to investigate mechanisms of T cell dysfunction beyond exhaustion. Indeed, emerging evidence positions T cell senescence, particularly within TILs, as a critical barrier to durable antitumor immunity. Senescence has been considered to be irreversible and associated with profound metabolic and functional impairment; however, strategies such as targeting ATM or MAPK signaling, have been able to prevent or reverse effector T cell senescence and exert synergistic effects when combined with checkpoint inhibitors, thus representing a promising therapeutic avenue [[102](https://www.cell.com/trends/endocrinology-metabolism/fulltext/S1043-2760(25)00190-0#)

102.

_J. Immunother. Cancer._ 2022; **10**

]. Moreover, advances in single-cell multi-omics and spatial transcriptomics now allow identification of novel cell populations and transitional T cell states within complex microenvironments. These technologies may enable the discovery of biomarkers to distinguish reversible dysfunction from irreversible senescence, offering potential targets to prevent T cells from reaching a terminal state (see Outstanding questions). A recent study found that NAD signatures in baseline peripheral blood mononuclear cells can predict CAR-T responses, suggesting that T cell metabolic profiles may serve as predictive biomarkers [[103](https://www.cell.com/trends/endocrinology-metabolism/fulltext/S1043-2760(25)00190-0#)

103.

_Nat. Can._ 2025;

]. Therefore, further research into the metabolic and epigenetic profiling of T cells as predictive biomarkers for CAR-T therapy outcomes is paramount.

Advances in CAR-T cell therapy demonstrate that enhancing metabolic resilience in the TME is key to maintaining T cell functionality. Notably, CAR-T cells engineered to target senescence-associated molecules, such as uPAR, have been shown to eliminate senescent cells and ameliorate age- and diet-related metabolic dysfunction [[104](https://www.cell.com/trends/endocrinology-metabolism/fulltext/S1043-2760(25)00190-0#)

104.

Amor, C. ...

**Prophylactic and long-lasting efficacy of senolytic CAR T cells against age-related metabolic dysfunction**

_Nat. Aging._ 2024; **4**:336-349

]. These findings suggest that dual-targeting CAR-T cells, engineered for both antitumor activity and clearance of senescent cells, could offer a novel strategy to overcome immunosuppressive barriers in the TME. Thus, future immunotherapies may move beyond exhaustion-centric models and incorporate senescence-targeted interventions (see Outstanding questions). Combining checkpoint blockade with metabolically adaptable, senescence-directed CAR-T cells may represent a next-generation approach to improve response rates and long-term outcomes in cancer immunotherapy.

Outstanding questions

Can we reverse T cell aging, and how do aging-related metabolic and epigenetic changes impact immune responses?

Do metabolic alterations drive the epigenetic changes associated with T cell senescence in the tumor microenvironment?

How can we target metabolic and epigenetic changes driving T cell exhaustion and senescence in tumors without affecting healthy T cells?

Are there reliable biomarkers to distinguish reversible dysfunction from irreversible senescence?

What metabolic or epigenetic T cell profiles could work as predictive biomarkers for therapeutic outcomes?

How can we integrate senescence-targeting interventions into future immunotherapies, moving beyond exhaustion-centric models?

## Glossary

**Cholesterol biosynthesis**process by which cells produce cholesterol, a critical lipid molecule required for maintaining cell membrane integrity, synthesizing steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D.

**_De novo fatty acid synthesis (FAS)_**metabolic pathway in which cells generate fatty acids from basic precursors, primarily acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA, rather than sourcing them from dietary intake or the breakdown of stored fat. FAS is crucial for producing LCFAs that are needed for building cell membranes, energy storage, and various signaling pathways.

**Glutaminolysis**this process involves the conversion of glutamine into metabolites that can enter the TCA cycle, facilitated by a series of enzymatic reactions. Glutaminase first catalyzes the conversion of glutamine to glutamate, which is subsequently processed into α-ketoglutarate via two separate pathways, thereby connecting glutamine metabolism to cellular energy production.

**Glycolysis**fundamental metabolic process where glucose is broken down to produce energy. This anaerobic pathway generates two molecules of pyruvate along with ATP, NADH, and water. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and proceeds independently of oxygen, serving as an essential energy-generating pathway for both aerobic and anaerobic organisms.

**Hexosamine biosynthetic pathway (HBP)**key pathway in glucose metabolism that acts as a glucose sensor across various tissues. HBP produces UDP-_N_-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc), a substrate for O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification.

**Immunological synapse**describes the highly organized, dynamic junction formed between a T lymphocyte (immune cell) and an antigen-presenting or target cell. The immunological synapse plays a crucial role in facilitating effective communication, ensuring that immune responses are specific and appropriately targeted.

**Lactylation**involves the attachment of lactate-derived groups to histones and non-histone proteins, underscoring lactate’s dual function as both a metabolic fuel and a signaling mediator. Histone lysine lactylation serves as an epigenetic mark, directly regulating gene expression by altering chromatin architecture.

**Oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)**mitochondrial pathway in which nutrients are oxidized to release chemical energy stored as ATP. This process relies on the coordinated function of five protein complexes (I–V), which drive ATP production through the ETC and the activity of ATP synthase.

3. **Summary Output for Summary**: Organize into a concise paragraph with logical flow, prioritizing clarity and judge the contribution of the information to the goal.

**Final Output Format using JSON format has "rational", "evidence", "summary" feilds**
